blocks.text: Between 1960 and 1966 Nigeria had a Prime Minister who sat in Parliament and could be voted out of office any afternoon. Since 1979 it has had a President who sits nowhere in the National Assembly and cannot be removed except by impeachment. Same country, two completely different machines.

blocks.markdown: The difference between these two systems is not about who is more powerful. It is about the **relationship between the executive and the legislature** — whether they are separated or fused.

blocks.title: The two systems in one sentence each
blocks.text: In a PRESIDENTIAL system the executive and the legislature are separately constituted, separately elected and separately answerable, with a President who is both Head of State and Head of Government. In a PARLIAMENTARY or CABINET system the executive is drawn from the legislature and remains continuously answerable to it, with a ceremonial Head of State separate from the Prime Minister who is Head of Government.

blocks.caption: The presidential and parliamentary systems compared

blocks.markdown:
### How Nigeria moved from one to the other

Under the **Independence Constitution of 1960** Nigeria operated a parliamentary system. Queen Elizabeth II was Head of State, represented in Nigeria by the Governor-General, Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe, while Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was Prime Minister and Head of Government.

When the **Republican Constitution of 1963** took effect on 1 October 1963, the link with the Crown was severed and Dr Azikiwe became Nigeria's first ceremonial President. Balewa remained Prime Minister, so the system was still parliamentary.

The **1979 Constitution** introduced the presidential system for the Second Republic, and the **1999 Constitution** retained it for the Fourth Republic. Since then Nigeria has had a directly elected President who is both Head of State and Head of Government, and under section 147 of the 1999 Constitution a minister who is a serving legislator must give up the legislative seat.

items: **Advantages of the presidential system** — stable fixed tenure, clear separation of powers, a single point of accountability, a President with a national mandate, and ministers chosen for competence rather than for holding a seat.
**Disadvantages of the presidential system** — risk of dictatorship if checks fail, deadlock when the President and legislature disagree, and slow removal of an incompetent President.

**Advantages of the parliamentary system** — rapid removal of a failing government, close co-operation between executive and legislature, ministers with legislative experience, and continuous scrutiny through question time.

**Disadvantages of the parliamentary system** — instability where no party has a firm majority, weak separation of powers, and a Prime Minister who can dominate the legislature through party discipline.

blocks.title: Identifying a system from constitutional provisions
blocks.prompt: A constitution provides that (i) the Head of State is elected by the whole nation for a fixed four-year term; (ii) ministers are appointed by the Head of State subject to legislative confirmation; (iii) a serving legislator appointed a minister must resign the seat; (iv) the Head of State may be removed only by impeachment for gross misconduct. Which system is this, and which provision is the strongest clue?

steps.text: Test the headship. One nationally elected office holding both ceremonial and executive functions points to a presidential system.
Test the tenure. A fixed term removable only by impeachment rules out the parliamentary vote of no confidence.

Test membership. Provision (iii) forcing a minister to vacate a legislative seat is the decisive clue: it enforces separation of personnel between the two organs, which a parliamentary system deliberately avoids.
Note the check that survives. Legislative confirmation of ministers in provision (ii) is a check and balance, not a fusion, so it is consistent with the presidential model.
Conclude: a presidential system, with provision (iii) as the strongest single indicator.

blocks.answer: A presidential system; the requirement that a minister resign a legislative seat is the strongest clue because it enforces separation of personnel between executive and legislature

blocks.title: Use the personnel test
blocks.text: If ministers sit in the legislature, the system is parliamentary. If they cannot, it is presidential. That one test decides most examination questions faster than any other, and it also explains the difference in how the executive is removed.

points: A presidential system separates executive and legislature; a parliamentary system fuses them.
In a presidential system the President is both Head of State and Head of Government and holds a fixed term.
In a parliamentary system a ceremonial Head of State is separate from the Prime Minister, who is removable by a vote of no confidence.
Nigeria was parliamentary from 1960 to 1966 and has been presidential since the 1979 Constitution.
In 1963 Nnamdi Azikiwe became ceremonial President while Abubakar Tafawa Balewa remained Prime Minister — the system was still parliamentary.
Presidential systems offer stability but risk deadlock; parliamentary systems offer flexibility but risk instability.
